after: ## From paragraph commentary to argument-wide commentary
alt: Three nested rings: evidence at the centre, the paragraph’s claim around it, and the thesis and next step on the outside. Three questions match the rings: what does it show (explain), how does it support this paragraph’s claim (relevance), and why does it matter for the thesis (significance).
caption: The first question is local; the third looks across the whole argument.

alt: A count of teenagers’ evening visits connects by one arrow to the paragraph claim that young people rely on evening hours (relevance) and by another to the thesis that libraries are essential public places (significance), because it shows the library serves people with nowhere else to go.
caption: Relevance links evidence to the paragraph; significance links it to the thesis.

after: ## Levels of commentary within an argument
alt: A schematic essay of two body paragraphs and a conclusion, with commentary lines colour-coded and linked to four levels: evidence-level commentary right after the evidence, paragraph-level at the end of a paragraph, bridge-level linking to the next paragraph, and thesis-level in the conclusion. Each has the lesson’s example.
caption: Evidence, paragraph, bridge and thesis levels keep the line of reasoning visible.

after: ## Techniques for keeping an argument connected
alt: A descending ladder starts from the survey figure (118 of 200 teenagers) and asks “So what?” three times: a quiet room is the condition of homework; shut hours take study away; the hours decide whether pupils keep up. It ends at the thesis that the library is the one place where people without money can belong.
caption: Keep asking “So what?” after each piece of evidence; stop when the answer reaches the thesis.

after: ## A public-domain example: Douglass's commentary on an occasion (1852)
alt: Two columns split Douglass’s sentences between the audience and the speaker: “yours” and “not mine”, “you may rejoice” and “I must mourn”, an inheritance “shared by you, not by me”, and sunlight bringing “life and healing” to them but “stripes and death” to him. Below, how the contrast serves relevance, significance and the speech’s driving question.
caption: Each sentence links an observation back to the question that drives the speech.

after: ## Worked example 1: commentary at four levels (written by Marlbridge)
alt: The library paragraph split into five labelled parts: the topic sentence, the survey evidence, evidence-level commentary explaining why a quiet room matters, paragraph-level commentary on keeping up, and a bridge-level question leading to the next paragraph on pensioners.
caption: Reading only the commentary should still give a clear path through the argument.
